title: Communication With Colleagues Standard
summary: Communication among colleagues must be clear, respectful, timely, professional, role-aware, and solution-focused — firm without being rude, direct without being aggressive.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, communication among colleagues must be clear, respectful, timely, professional, role-aware, and solution-focused.

How therapists communicate with one another affects teamwork, leadership, task execution, client service, accountability, escalation, information flow, workplace peace, and the overall Zura Spa culture.
Professional communication does not mean that everybody communicates in exactly the same way.
At Zura Spa, the appropriate communication approach depends partly on the professional relationship and responsibility between the people communicating.
A leader may need to give a firm instruction. A non-leader may need to respectfully suggest an alternative. Two colleagues at the same level may communicate directly and clearly.
The standard is not that every conversation must sound soft. The standard is that communication must remain: CLEAR → APPROPRIATE → RESPECTFUL → PROFESSIONAL → ACTIONABLE.

sections.title: 1. The Communication Mindset
paragraphs: Every therapist should have the mindset: "My words should help the team understand, coordinate, correct, solve, and move forward."
I can be firm without being rude.
I can disagree without becoming disrespectful.
I can correct without humiliating.
I can receive correction without becoming defensive.
I can ask a question without challenging authority disrespectfully.
I can give an instruction without belittling another person.
I can raise a concern without creating unnecessary conflict.
I can communicate directly without becoming aggressive.
At Zura Spa, communication should move work forward. It should not create another problem while trying to solve one.

sections.title: 2. Why Communication With Colleagues Matters
paragraphs: Good colleague communication supports teamwork, smooth operations, leadership coordination, problem-solving, workplace peace, and client experience.

sections.title: Teamwork
paragraphs: Therapists often depend on one another for massage preparation, 4-hands massage, client handovers, task execution, room readiness, Freshen-Up routines, assessments, session updates, cleaning, stock management, client departure, and other operational responsibilities.
Poor communication in one area can affect several people.

sections.title: Smooth Operations
paragraphs: Clear communication helps the team know who is responsible, what needs to happen, what has already happened, what is still pending, who needs to act next, and whether there is a blocker.

sections.title: Leadership Coordination
paragraphs: The Zura Spa team has different leadership responsibilities. Communication should respect those roles so that instructions are clear, responsibilities are understood, decisions are not constantly challenged through disorderly communication, and leaders remain open to useful information from team members.

sections.title: Problem-Solving
paragraphs: Good communication allows issues to be addressed early.
Instead of Assumption → Anger → Gossip → Conflict, the expected flow is: OBSERVE → ASK → CLARIFY → COMMUNICATE → SOLVE → ESCALATE IF NECESSARY.

sections.title: Workplace Peace
paragraphs: Professional communication reduces arguments, misunderstandings, gossip, silent resentment, cliques, and unnecessary confrontation.
Workplace peace does not mean nobody disagrees. It means disagreements are handled professionally.

sections.title: Client Experience
paragraphs: The client may never hear the full internal conversation. But they may experience the result.

Poor communication can lead to delays, missed client requests, poor co-therapist synchronization, wrong instructions, missed tasks, unprepared rooms, confused front desk, and poor departure experience.
Internal communication eventually becomes external service quality.

sections.title: 3. Zura Spa Communication Structure
paragraphs: The following communication approaches apply according to role and responsibility.

sections.title: A. Executive Director (E.D.) to Staff Members — Directive / Demand
paragraphs: The E.D. reserves the right to give directives, instructions, requirements, decisions, and demands connected to legitimate business responsibility.

Where the E.D. gives a clear work directive, the expectation is that it is understood and carried out, except where the instruction is unclear, there is a genuine safety concern, there is an operational blocker, or clarification is required.
A directive does not require the E.D. to phrase every instruction as a request.
Example: "Thr. Jane, complete the stock count and post the report before 4 PM." This is appropriate.
However, directive authority does not mean permission to insult, humiliate, threaten, or degrade staff. Leadership authority and respectful conduct can exist together.

sections.title: B. Leader to Leader — Respectful + Appealing + Professional
paragraphs: Leaders should communicate with one another as partners responsible for coordinating the organization.
Examples include communication between Manager, SM, CM, SP, LT, and TG.
The tone should be respectful and collaborative.
Examples: "CM, please can we have Client Sam's handover before the therapists proceed?" or "LT, can you please review the assessment before we close it?"
Leaders should avoid communicating as though they are competing for authority. The objective is: COORDINATE, NOT COMPETE.

sections.title: C. Leader to Non-Leader — Firm + Clear + Open to Relevant Suggestions
paragraphs: A leader should be able to give a clear instruction.
Example: "Thr. Jane, please complete the Freshen-Up Routine before Client Sam proceeds to the room."
The instruction should be clear, specific, professional, and firm where necessary.
At the same time, leadership should remain open when the therapist has relevant information.
Example: "SP, I understand. The only issue is that Room 2 is currently occupied. Can I use Room 3 instead?"
The leader should consider reasonable information without treating every suggestion as insubordination.
Firm leadership does not mean "Nobody can speak." It means "The responsibility and expected outcome are clear."

sections.title: D. Non-Leader to Leader — Suggestive + Respectful
paragraphs: A non-leader may ask questions, give useful information, raise concerns, suggest solutions, disagree professionally, and ask for clarification.
However, the communication should recognize the leader's role.
Examples: "SP, may I suggest that we use Room 3 so the client does not have to wait?" or "LT, please can you clarify the correct transition for this routine?"
Not: "No, that's not what we're doing."
Where the therapist believes an instruction creates a genuine issue, the correct approach is respectful clarification or escalation.

sections.title: E. Non-Leader to Non-Leader — Direct + Clear + Respectful
paragraphs: Colleagues at the same level should not need unnecessary formality to communicate normal work matters.
Examples: "Thr. Jane, please send the Massage Start update." "Thr. Clara, Client Sam requested water." "Please confirm when Room 2 is ready."
Direct communication is appropriate. However, direct does not mean aggressive, commanding unnecessarily, insulting, or disrespectful.

sections.title: 4. Role Does Not Remove Respect
paragraphs: The communication structure establishes order, not human superiority.
A leader is not permitted to insult, humiliate, belittle, mock, or threaten unnecessarily because they hold a role.
Similarly, a non-leader cannot use "We are all equal" as a reason to disregard professional authority or instructions.
DIFFERENT ROLES → DIFFERENT RESPONSIBILITIES → SAME DIGNITY.

sections.title: 5. Communication Procedure
paragraphs: When communicating a work matter, therapists should generally follow this process.

sections.title: Step 1 — Know Who You Are Speaking To
paragraphs: Ask: Is this the E.D., a leader, or a colleague at my level? Adjust the communication appropriately.

sections.title: Step 2 — Know Why You Are Communicating
paragraphs: Are you giving an instruction, giving an update, asking a question, reporting, correcting, escalating, suggesting, or requesting support? The purpose should determine the message.

sections.title: Step 3 — State the Matter Clearly
paragraphs: Avoid making colleagues decode vague communication.
Instead of "What is happening?" where more context is needed, say: "Thr. Jane, has the Freshen-Up Routine for Client Sam been completed?"

sections.title: Step 4 — Include the Expected Action
paragraphs: Where action is needed, say what should happen.
Example: "Thr. Jane, please complete Room 2 setup and post Task Completion Report on the Task Wall."

sections.title: Step 5 — Listen to Relevant Response
paragraphs: If the other person provides clarification, a blocker, important information, or a reasonable alternative, listen before reacting.

sections.title: Step 6 — Confirm Understanding Where Necessary
paragraphs: For important responsibilities, confirm: "Understood." or "Please confirm once completed." This reduces assumption.

sections.title: Step 7 — Use the Appropriate Channel
paragraphs: Where the matter requires a WhatsApp wall update, task report, escalation, client update, or leadership notification, use the correct channel.
A private conversation does not automatically replace an official update.

sections.title: 6. Communication During Task Execution
paragraphs: Task communication should generally follow: ASSIGN → ACKNOWLEDGE → EXECUTE → UPDATE → REPORT → REVIEW → CLOSE.
If Thr. Jane is assigned "Thr. Jane, prepare Room 2," the appropriate response is not silence.
Where acknowledgement is required: "Understood."
After completion: "Room 2 preparation completed. Bed laid, towels ready, supplies checked. Room ready for client."
This supports the Task Completion Report Standard.

sections.title: 7. Communication During 4-Hands Massage
paragraphs: Co-therapists should communicate in ways that support synchronization, client comfort, smooth transitions, and shared responsibilities.
Communication should be brief, quiet, necessary, and professional.
Do not argue over the client, correct the co-therapist loudly, hold personal conversations, compete for control, or display personal tension.
Where an operational discussion is needed, handle it discreetly.

sections.title: 8. Correcting a Colleague
paragraphs: Correction should normally focus on: WHAT HAPPENED → WHAT THE STANDARD REQUIRES → WHAT NEEDS TO CHANGE.
Example: "Thr. Jane, after cleaning the client's feet, please remember that the Massage Start Routine requires us to wash our hands again before beginning."
Not: "You never listen. You always do things wrong."
Correct the behaviour. Do not attack the person's identity.

sections.title: 9. Receiving Correction
paragraphs: When corrected: listen, understand the issue, ask for clarification where necessary, correct the behaviour, and avoid immediate defensiveness.
An appropriate response may simply be: "Understood. I'll correct it."
You may respectfully explain relevant context. But explanation should not automatically become resistance.

sections.title: 10. Communication During Disagreement
paragraphs: Disagreement is allowed. Disrespect is not.
When you disagree: PAUSE → LISTEN → CLARIFY → STATE YOUR VIEW → SEEK RESOLUTION.
Example: "LT, I understand the instruction. My concern is that Client Sam specifically requested a female therapist. Can we confirm with CM before proceeding?"
This communicates disagreement without challenging the person disrespectfully.

sections.title: 11. When Direct Communication Is Not Working
paragraphs: If the conversation becomes hostile, the issue keeps repeating, the parties cannot resolve it, someone refuses to listen, the matter involves misconduct, or the issue requires authority — stop extending the argument.
ESCALATE. Do not attempt to win every disagreement. The objective is resolution.

sections.title: 12. What Good Communication Looks Like
paragraphs: Good communication sounds like:
"Thr. Jane, please update Massage Start."
"SP, I have a blocker. The room is not ready because clean towels are unavailable."
"CM, Client Sam requested water."
"LT, I understand. May I suggest another approach?"
"SM, task completed and report posted on the Task Wall."
"Thr. Clara, please can you clarify what you meant?"
It is short, clear, professional, relevant, and actionable.

sections.title: 13. What the Opposite Looks Like
paragraphs: The opposite is communication that produces confusion, hostility, or disorder.

sections.title: Shouting
paragraphs: Volume is used instead of clarity.

sections.title: Sarcasm
paragraphs: Example: "Madam Supervisor, since you know everything…" The title may be correct, but the tone is disrespectful.

sections.title: Silent Treatment
paragraphs: A therapist is offended and stops giving necessary work information.

sections.title: Public Humiliation
paragraphs: Someone is corrected loudly in front of clients or colleagues when private correction would have been appropriate.

sections.title: Gossip
paragraphs: The therapist discusses the problem with everybody except the person or leader who can resolve it.

sections.title: Passive Aggression
paragraphs: Examples: "Do whatever you like." "Since you're the boss." "No problem, you'll see." These messages create tension without solving anything.

sections.title: Withholding Information
paragraphs: A therapist intentionally does not provide an update because they are upset with someone.

sections.title: Aggressive Directness
paragraphs: Direct communication becomes "Go and do it now!" from someone without the appropriate authority or context.

sections.title: Challenging Leadership Disrespectfully
paragraphs: A therapist responds "You cannot tell me what to do" instead of respectfully clarifying or escalating.

sections.title: Leadership Bullying
paragraphs: A leader communicates "Because I'm your leader, you must keep quiet." That is also against the standard.

sections.title: 14. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate Poor Colleague Communication
paragraphs: Poor communication affects far more than the two people involved. It can create client service failure, team division, misunderstandings, missed tasks, delays, cliques, resentment, leadership breakdown, emotional tension, poor handovers, and escalating conflicts.

Zura Spa will therefore not normalize shouting, insults, humiliation, gossip, silent treatment, withholding operational information, repeatedly challenging leadership disrespectfully, leadership using authority to bully, aggressive confrontation, or workplace communication being controlled by friendship or personal conflict.

sections.title: 15. Impact on the Team
paragraphs: Poor communication creates rework, micromanagement, distrust, cliques, emotional exhaustion, and can weaken leadership or team voice.

If instructions are unclear, tasks may need to be repeated. If leaders cannot rely on updates, they begin chasing everyone. When information is intentionally withheld, colleagues stop trusting one another.
People begin communicating only with those they like. This conflicts with the Zura Spa standard: We are not friends or family at work — we are a team.
Constant arguments make the workplace tiring even when the physical workload is manageable. If every instruction turns into confrontation, team coordination becomes difficult.
If leaders never listen to useful information from non-leaders, important operational knowledge is lost. Good hierarchy should create order without silencing useful input.

sections.title: 16. Impact on the Client
paragraphs: The client may experience poor internal communication as therapists arriving late, missed water requests, wrong service information, unprepared rooms, therapists disagreeing during massage, poor synchronization, delayed departure, or staff appearing confused.
The client does not need to know whose communication failed. They simply experience: "Zura Spa was disorganized."

sections.title: 17. What Therapists Should Do
list: Address colleagues by approved work names or roles.
Separate personal feelings from professional communication.

sections.title: 18. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Correct colleagues unnecessarily in front of clients.
Use leadership authority to silence all suggestions.
Speak to non-leaders as though they are inferior people.
Refuse to communicate because of friendship conflict.
Turn every disagreement into an escalation.
Continue an argument when escalation is more appropriate.
Communicate important operational matters only privately when they belong on the approved WhatsApp wall.

sections.title: 19. Communication and Accountability
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: Clear instruction + acknowledgement + execution = professional coordination. Respectful correction + changed behaviour = growth. Disagreement + professional discussion = maturity. Blocker + early communication = accountability.

But: Repeatedly ignoring operational communication = performance concern. Deliberately withholding necessary information = accountability concern. Repeated disrespectful communication = conduct concern. Threatening, humiliating or bullying colleagues = serious conduct concern. Deliberately allowing communication failure to affect a client = serious performance/accountability concern.

sections.title: 20. Quick Communication Structure

items.label: Leader → Non-Leader
items.body: Firm and clear, while open to relevant suggestions

sections.closing: These structures exist to promote order, accountability, respect, coordination, clarity, effective leadership, and teamwork.

sections.title: 21. The Zura Spa Communication Standard
paragraphs: KNOW THE ROLE → CHOOSE THE APPROACH → SPEAK CLEARLY → LISTEN → CLARIFY → ACT → UPDATE → ESCALATE IF NECESSARY

DIRECT DOES NOT MEAN RUDE. FIRM DOES NOT MEAN AGGRESSIVE. RESPECTFUL DOES NOT MEAN WEAK. SUGGESTIVE DOES NOT MEAN AFRAID. LEADERSHIP DOES NOT MEAN DISRESPECT. DISAGREEMENT DOES NOT MEAN CONFLICT. CORRECTION DOES NOT MEAN HUMILIATION. FRIENDSHIP DOES NOT CHANGE THE COMMUNICATION STANDARD.
We do not communicate according to mood, friendship, anger, or ego. We communicate according to role, responsibility, professionalism, and the needs of the team.
A strong team is not one where nobody disagrees. A strong team is one where people can communicate, disagree, correct, listen, clarify, solve, report, and continue working together professionally.
SPEAK WITH PURPOSE. LISTEN WITH MATURITY. RESPECT THE ROLE. PROTECT THE TEAM. MAINTAIN THE ZURA STANDARD.

remember: Speak with purpose. Listen with maturity. Respect the role. Communicate according to responsibility — not mood, friendship, or ego.
